title: Who Is the Right Person to Make the Decision
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article dissects the 'meta-decision' of who should own a delegated decision, weighing several intuitive but flawed criteria, deepest expertise, most affected party, and best consensus-builder, against their respective downsides. It settles on three factors the best leaders actually weigh: whether the person has the bandwidth to give the decision real attention, whether they understand the affected stakeholders, and, most tellingly, whether the leader already senses the person's instincts align with where the decision should land. The piece is candid that leaders often quietly select decision-makers whose judgment they already trust to reach the outcome they'd want.
points: The article frames 'who should decide' as its own meta-decision worth weighing carefully.
Common criteria (deepest expertise, most affected party, best consensus-builder) all carry real downsides.
Three factors the best leaders weigh: bandwidth, stakeholder understanding, and alignment with the leader's own instincts.
The piece is candid that leaders often select decision-makers whose judgment already tracks their own.
quotes: The “right” person usually makes a world of difference. So, what goes into making this meta-decision (the decision about who decides) is worth weighing seriously.
But those with an in-depth working knowledge of the issues often overplay their expertise and allow their pre-existing biases to influence the decision process and outcome.
More important than expertise or track record, good leaders depend on others who have the bandwidth to spend the necessary time to reach a quality outcome.
Without saying so, they often select a decision-maker they believe is already close to where they think the decision should land.
When it comes to delegating important decisions, good leaders put a thumb on the scale.
